Yet these persons cannot declare themselves or make themselves known by name. Consequently, there can be no possibility—much less any obligation—of knowing who they are individually. The Imam's instruction to refer henceforth to the sages who know and transmit the Imams' sayings and teachings concerns a category of people. It does not designate any individual among them, or publicly invest anyone by name with a superior rank.

During the ghaybat, it is impossible to know which of the Perfect Shiites is the Bâb and nâ'ib. This is the precise force of a hadîth transmitted by Mofazzal: “The Bâb of the Twelfth Imam is concealed by the very fact of the Twelfth Imam's concealment.” Everything written about the necessity of knowing these guides and about their mediating role must therefore be understood as requiring knowledge of their spiritual category, not knowledge of them as individually identifiable persons who have been appointed by name (pp. 110–111). The endless and pointless controversies surrounding the fourth pillar arose from a failure to grasp this essential distinction.

This spiritual category of higher beings ultimately embraces the whole hidden hierarchy familiar from Sufism: the qotb (pole), the awtâd (the stakes supporting the “cosmic tent”), the abdâl (the substitutes or those who succeed one another), the nojabâ and noqabâ (the spiritual Nobles and Princes). This hierarchy rests on certain hadîths and is claimed as an integral part of the Shiite idea, which Sufism, on this account, merely adopted. Shaykhi thought is concerned above all with a twofold hierarchy: the Nojabâ and Noqabâ, the spiritual Nobles and Princes. The fourth pillar calls for acknowledging their existence as a whole.

The Shaykhis have never said or claimed that any of their shaykhs was the Imam's particular Naqîb or Bâb. Certainly, insofar as the category of Awliyâ also includes all learned people whose guidance believers follow, there is no reason why Shaykhi scholars should not belong to it. In that case, however, membership is only a general attribute, just as one might say “Zayd is just.” During the occultation, no one can be designated and recognized as “the first person after the Imam”—that is, as the Bâb, exercising an office to which the qualification Nâtiq wâhid would be publicly and visibly attached. We shall explain that expression shortly.

The reason things must be so lies in the very nature of the ghaybat, whose meaning the Shaykhis seem to have explored with exceptional depth. The Imam is the “Hidden Imam” essentially because of a condition of human consciousness: human beings have veiled him from themselves and made themselves incapable of knowing and recognizing him (pp. 115 ff.). His manifestation is inconceivable, we might say, because the necessary conditions for that manifestation to be perceived do not exist. How could he show himself to people who cannot see him? “The time has not yet come.” As Mofazzal's hadîth teaches, his concealment entails the concealment of his Bâb and, consequently, of all the Perfect Ones from ordinary people.

Were they to announce themselves, they would confront humanity with a choice it is not capable of making. They would be arrested or banished; alternatively, the choice would degenerate into wretched rivalries and personal ambitions. For the day when the decisive choice is laid bare is precisely the day of the final manifestation. What the Shaykhis have affirmed, then, is that these higher beings, the “Perfect Shiites” (Kâmilân-e Shî'a), must exist, and that their existence must be known. They have never meant that these beings must manifest themselves, still less that one must recognize a supposed public manifestation of them (ibid.).

We can therefore say that, on this point, Shaykhi thought has carried a fundamental Shiite insight to its limit. What it gives us is a phenomenology of the ghaybat: an account of concealment and invisible form as conditions of spiritual experience. If the Imam, the first and last divine manifestation, is now the Hidden Imam, this is not because of some external event that suddenly took place on a particular day in the past. The death of the last nâ'ib merely marks a point of reference. The transition from minor to major occultation marks a reversal in humanity's lived experience of time: the time of presence becomes the time of absence.

Human beings themselves have veiled the Imam from their sight. They have become incapable of seeing him, having paralyzed or lost the organs that perceive divine manifestations, the organs of the dimensio mystica. This is why neither the Imam nor his companions can appear openly, publicly, and without a veil. Such an appearance would require human beings to possess a faculty of perception through which they could recognize the Imam and his companions when they became visible.

But humanity, in its present condition—whatever explanation we may give for that condition—so completely lacks such a faculty that any public declaration by a person claiming to be the Imam's Bâb, let alone the Imam himself, takes the form of an imposture. It is precisely this deception against which the Imam warned his followers in his final message to his last deputy.

After these explanations, there should be no ambiguity left concerning the fourth pillar, and therefore none concerning the idea in which it culminates: wahdat-e Nâtiq, the oneness of the one who speaks. This gives Shaykh Sarkâr Âghâ an opportunity to make certain observations that deserve our attention. They concern the entire Shaykhi position and reveal his reservations about the future of a spiritual Islam. This final theme had been discussed in detail by Shaykh Mohammad Karîm-Khân Kermânî and was not new: his predecessors had also addressed it.

But it is a difficult technical question, not readily understood by ordinary people. It comes from traditions (akhbâr) that ordinary believers rarely have occasion even to hear about. It should therefore never have been discussed outside the circle of specialists in hikmat ilâhîya, divine wisdom, rather than being exploited by agitators.

There are, besides, many religious questions still unresolved, or whose solutions are far from having become established certainties. They remain matters for inquiry, the work of the ahl-e nazar, those who pursue intellectual investigation. Questions on which there has been settled agreement since the beginnings of Islam are very few, and even those have often taken several generations to settle. If we believed our critics, the shaykh declares, ordinary people, the untrained ('awâmm), would have to be regarded as more learned than scholars, simply because they agree among themselves about their accepted, ready-made convictions while scholars disagree.

We would then have to adopt the opinions of the crowd and forget the prophets and sages, together with all the research invited by teachings that have yet to be explored (pp. 120–122). This solemn protest against conformism merits our attention. Against the paralysis of thought, so often regarded as a fate hanging over Islam, it sets the determination to carry every question beyond its present limits, a continual spiritual reformation whose aims are broader than those of any program of social reform.

As for the final idea, wahdat-e Nâtiq, in which the fourth pillar culminates, its meaning follows from everything we have said. The technical term nâtiq, “the one who speaks,” belongs to the familiar language of Shiite tradition. It is especially well established in Ismaili gnosis, where it carries a particular nuance. That there is only one (wâhid) who speaks can be understood only in the light of our preceding discussion of the hierarchy of “Perfect Shiites,” a hierarchy invisible during the Imam's occultation.

The word nâtiq can describe the Imam as one who “speaks” in God's name or in the Prophet's name. In that case the sâmit, the “silent” Imam, is the one who comes after him. Generally speaking, each of the Twelve Imams was nâtiq during his own time as Imam, while his future successor remained the sâmit, or “silent” Imam (p. 124). The term can also be applied to certain Shiites, describing them as “Perfect Ones” (kâmilûn, bozorgvârân). Examples include Salmân Pârsî and those like him: mirrors reflecting the image of the Imam whose Bâb they were, guiding others in his name and toward him. The term nâtiq, in this usage, also has a proper or literal meaning and a figurative meaning.

We shall return to the latter at the end. In its proper sense, the nâtiq are the Imams and the prophets; in turn, the most eminent of the Shiites—the most learned and spiritually perfected—have also been nâtiq. Among that elite, the one who, by virtue of his spiritual qualification, was the “first person after the Imam,” the Bâb-e a'zâm, was in the proper sense the nâtiq of the Shiites. In relation to him, the others were sâmit: silent.

What the Shaykhi masters have affirmed is that, by the Imam's arrangement, “there is a Salmân in every age.” In their terminology he is called nâtiq, and there is only one such nâtiq (wâhid), because he is the Perfect Individual (fard-e kâmil), the foremost among the Shiites. He is their center, the earthly pole or nadir of the Imam, who is the heavenly pole.

In relation to the Imam, he is like a burning wick whose fire is nothing but the communication of an invisible Fire. He corresponds to the heart in relation to the human body. These statements, of course, make sense only in the light of a belief accepted throughout Shiism: that there exist higher beings, the Nojabâ and Noqabâ, mentioned above. Their hierarchy among human beings rests entirely upon their inward spiritual worth, their closeness to the Imam. They may never claim it as a title, publicly display it, or use it for any worldly purpose. The shaykhs in the Shaykhi line of transmission (silsila) have therefore affirmed that in every age there exists this Nâtiq wâhid, the “Perfect Shiite” and supreme Bâb of the Imam.

But not one of them has ever claimed to be that person or demanded recognition as such. Quite the contrary. They have affirmed his existence because the human world, earthly humanity, cannot be without him. They have equally affirmed that he cannot be publicly manifested: human beings cannot identify him, single him out, or proclaim his name and person. His name and identity remain the Imam's secret, for the very reasons already given, bound up with the nature of the ghaybat and the time of the ghaybat (pp. 127–131).

Mofazzal's hadîth thus has strict and decisive consequences. Anyone who publicly proclaims himself the Imam's Bâb thereby places himself outside Shiism, because he profanes its fundamental secret, violates the occultation, and breaks with the expectation of the final revelation. No school has argued this point more forcefully than the Shaykhis. This is why Bábism and the Bahá'í faith, whatever interest they may have as religious phenomena in their own right, can appear from this standpoint only as the very negation of Shaykhi thought.

To derive them from Shaykh Ahmad Ahsâ'î is a mistaken perception of spiritual relationships, or an unjustified claim of descent. It requires considerable inattention and a serious lack of philosophical experience to think otherwise. More importantly, this very point helps explain why Shaykhi thought, although its 'irfân (mystical knowledge) so often speaks the same language as Sufism, nevertheless takes a stand against Sufism—or, more precisely, against the Sufi understanding of the role and authority of the shaykh. The issue arises insofar as the shaykh of a tarîqat, a Sufi order, tends to be recognized by that order as the Imam's visible nâ'ib, and to assume that role openly, in his own name and person.

This distinction must not be forgotten when we speak of the relationship between Shiism and Sufism. A remark recounted to me in Tehran some twelve years ago by an excellent friend who knew these matters well casts a particularly clear light on it. An eminent shaykh of Qom, Hajj Sayyed Mahdî Qawâm, used to tell his students: “Certainly you must be 'orafâ—people who know mystical theosophy—and practice tasawwof, Sufi spirituality.

“But take great care never to enter a tarîqat, a Sufi order. You must not bind yourself or submit to any shaykh. In binding yourself to him, you inevitably bind yourself also to the limits of his person and his spiritual horizon. The mystical Shiite ('irfânî) must choose the Imam himself—one of the holy Imams—directly as his only Qotb, his only spiritual pole, and follow this personal guide directly, without an intermediary.” All spiritual teaching is thus centered on the search for, and encounter with, an invisible personal master (ostâd-e ghaybî), who is the Imam. We have seen an exemplary instance of this in Shaykh Ahmad Ahsâ'î's life. If we ask what form Shiite spirituality takes, I know of no more illuminating answer. The personal encounter with the Imam may occur in a dream or in a waking vision.

We shall explain later (Book VII) how such an encounter is possible without in any way weakening the strict conditions of the ghaybat. For the conditions of the Manifestation do not yet exist. The time of the parousia, the Imam's final appearance, has not yet come. Or rather, that appearance is the culminating act of an eschatology—a movement toward the final unveiling—that must not simply burst upon the world unexpectedly on some distant day, but must be fulfilled within and through the very time of the occultation. The ripening of the Imam's final revelation through the time of his hiddenness: this is the “meaning of history” when the Imam's history is understood as the history of Shiite consciousness. It is the growth of his inward presence in the hearts of his followers, as their invisible guide and master.

This last point brings us to a final question, one that both complements and sums up the matters considered here, since its answer involves all the fundamental positions we have surveyed. The Shaykhis have been asked how and why they, in particular, felt called to reveal and affirm the fourth pillar. Clearly, they cannot try to justify by any chain of causes what they experience essentially as a divine gift.

But they have understood both its meaning and its imperative in the light of the fundamental Paraclete idea of Shiism: the Imam's final epiphany as the Paraclete will disclose the hidden meaning of every religious Revelation. The Shaykhi conviction is that Shiism contains a multitude of teachings still concealed, and that the reason for their concealment—the obstacle to making them known—lies not with God but with human beings. The historical circumstances of the Shiites certainly made taqîyeh, the prudent concealment of one's beliefs, necessary.

Even when circumstances became outwardly more favorable, especially from the Safavid period onward, official stability encouraged an almost exclusive concern with the outward meaning of the transmitted reports (akhbâr) and with fiqh, legal scholarship, which degenerated into case-by-case casuistry and formalism. The fundamental metaphysical questions—those concerning walâyat, haqîqat (spiritual truth), and ma'rifat (spiritual knowledge)—were so neglected that it remained impossible to examine them without observing a certain esotericism and practicing taqîyeh.
But the time of the ghaybat is precisely a time in which this veil of secrecy is gradually lifted. The unveiling of the fourth pillar is one example.

Esotericism thus becomes here a principle of movement and progress: a progress that constitutes the very meaning of an eschatology already unfolding, from the mission of the “last Prophet” to the final appearance of the last Imam. Consequently—and this is Shaykh Sarkâr Âghâ's conclusion—instead of suspecting the Shaykhi masters of claiming for themselves a status that their entire conduct rejects, we should read their books and consider why they have, on the contrary, condemned anyone who makes the absurd claim to be recognized as one of the Nojabâ or Noqabâ (pp. 132 ff.). Their aim was to bring a theologoumenon, a theological idea, into the light, not to designate some particular person by name, since that would contradict the very conditions of the ghaybat.

Far from claiming this distinction for themselves, they have exposed the absurdity of every such claim. They have warded off a danger that always remains possible within Shiism, precisely by placing this spiritual qualification on the plane of existence and level of consciousness demanded by the Imam's occultation. In one sense, we might say, nothing could be more esoteric than the Shaykhi position, since the structure and hierarchy of the Shiite community remain “secret,” suprasensible, and invisible.

Yet nothing provides a better antidote to the claims of every counterfeit esotericism. The Nojabâ and Noqabâ belong to “another world.” They may nevertheless live in this one, dressed as craftsmen, farmers, or simply as scholars (p. 137).

But they can give no outward sign of their invisible rank that would lead to their recognition in this world, on worldly terms. And if someone happened to recognize one of them, that person would have no right to betray the secret. Each of them, we might say, is bound by the strict law of the Knights of the Grail: “... and his power remains sacred so long as he remains unknown to all.”

The misfortune is that here, more than anywhere, Shiite esotericism far exceeds ordinary awareness and the assumptions people commonly accept as settled. It has happened that the word nâtiq was taken not in its proper Shaykhi sense but in the merely figurative sense (majâz) mentioned earlier. Because the oneness of the Nâtiq was then understood as applying to scholars in general—scholars of the outward law ('olamâ-ye zâhirî)—critics concluded that the Shaykhi doctrine meant there could be only one such scholar in each age.

We can understand the alarm caused by this mistake, but it would be frankly comic if it were not also a rather serious symptom. Much needless speaking and writing were required to explain that the number of outward religious scholars, the 'olamâ-ye zâhirî, has always been unlimited in every age (p. 140).

Our account of the Shaykhi school has necessarily been brief. Still, we hope it has suggested the complexity and extraordinary richness of its theosophy, and the importance of its place in Shiite thought. We hope, too, that it will help dispel certain hasty judgments about the school—judgments which, alas, abound in the history of philosophy whenever that history is not written from firsthand study.
4. Eschatology and the Correspondence of Time and Space

To conclude, we should insist on one further point. It will allow us to begin comparing two schools of Shiite thought, while extending the eschatological perspective that has just opened before us. In ordinary theological usage, “eschatology” refers to the events of the end (eschaton): the end of this time, of our Aeon. Viewed within chronological time, eschatology is therefore essentially a matter of waiting; hence the Hidden Imam is called the “Expected Imam.”

But every departure from the dimension of chronological time is, in that very sense, also an eschatological event. All hierognosis, all visionary perception, is eschatological, because it brings to an end the conditions of time as measured by the chronology of this world. We saw a striking example in the tradition of the White Cloud, as interpreted by Qâzî Sa'îd Qommî. To be capable of perceiving spiritual forms is already to belong to their world, to have stepped, even if only momentarily, outside the “opaque and dense” time of this world.

When the Shaykhis call the perception of the dimensio mystica—the malakûtî, or spiritual dimension—“seeing things in Hûrqalyâ,” they mean a kind of eschatological vision. An eschatology that is not simply an event destined to occur without warning on some distant day, but is already being fulfilled in the present, implies the capacity to “see things in Hûrqalyâ.” It means perceiving here and now, through their mystical dimension, the whole reality of beings and things—of which chronological succession allows us to perceive only a part at any given moment.

Hûrqalyâ is the highest of the three “emerald cities” beyond Mount Qâf, a name we first encountered in the work of Suhrawardi. Hûrqalyâ is the mundus imaginalis, the imaginal world, the world of imaginal forms and archetypal images. Beings and things “seen in Hûrqalyâ” possess the depth of a mirror. This does not mean that such vision is an inferior form of knowledge, still awaiting a higher, face-to-face encounter. Rather than recalling Saint Paul's words, velut in speculo, “as in a mirror,” should suggest here the true, original meaning of all speculative mysticism: a form of spiritual insight grounded in the mirror.

Without that transparency, not only does the real relation between the suprasensible and the sensible remain unseen; so does the interrelation of all the universes, which serve one another as mirrors, as “places of epiphany” (mazhar). Vision in speculo, “in the mirror,” begins as soon as the perspective of suprasensible Forms opens, beyond the conditions of “opaque and dense” time. This is why we have emphasized the fascination that the laws of optics held for our medieval metaphysicians of light. The degree to which a person can perceive things “in Hûrqalyâ” depends on the degree of esoteric knowledge attained. In other words, the degree of spiritual consciousness depends on how close one has come to the place of Return, which is also the place of Origin.

To Shaykh Mohammad Karîm-Khân Kermânî, Shaykh Ahmad Ahsâ'î's second successor, we owe a striking way of giving form to this idea. We should begin by recalling it. It will then be easier to understand the isomorphism—the correspondence in form—between patterns in time and patterns in space that arises within the eschatological perspective we have just defined, a perspective in which the thought of Shaykhi theosophers and that of Ismaili Shiite theosophers converge.

We spoke earlier of an eschatology—an unfolding of the last things—“already taking place since the mission of the last prophet came to an end.” It would be more accurate, following a passage by Shaykh Mohammad Karîm-Khân Kermânî, to say “since the very beginning of the cycle of prophecy.” That takes us back to Adam himself, “the earthly Adam” (not the “Greater Adam,” the Homo maximus discussed earlier).

Adam, “our father,” was the first of the seven great prophets, the prophet of the first of the seven periods making up the “cycle of prophecy.” Two words, mabda' and ma'âd—origin and return—name the two great acts of a drama that can also be called cosmogony and prophetology. The first act is the “descent” of the Intelligence (Ennoia) into the earthly world: the cycle in which the cosmos comes into being.

The second is the Intelligence's “ascent,” taking our world upward with it. That ascent begins with the cycle of prophecy, inaugurated by Adam. The lowest point reached by the descending Intelligence coincided with Adam's appearance. “Then, through him and through all those who call people to God, this summons rang out in the world: Now turn around and return.”

Here we meet a characteristically Gnostic vision once again. Shaykhi spiritual philosophy also describes the history of a world in what might be called a “Gothic style”: its governing axis is vertical, not the horizontal prospect of limitless evolution. This is not a history made up of irreversible outward events. Rather, history's very advance is a turning back toward its origin.

Seen in terms of form, what is repeated on the scale of an entire world seems to correspond to the “miracle of the octave” to which we referred earlier when explaining the law of spiritual interpretation (Book I, Chapter II, section 4). “During the Descent,” our shaykh writes, “God's guarantors were the cosmic utterances through which the cosmos came into being. During the Ascent, they are the inspired utterances of the language of prophecy.

“Through the prophetic speech of the Messengers, the world begins to ascend, to make its gradual return. If the ages of the past should be disclosed to you, you will see them beneath your feet, arranged vertically—not beside you, not ahead or behind you on a horizontal plane.”

This is precisely where our familiar way of thinking about history is liable to lose its footing. “The story of our world,” the shaykh writes, “is the story of a man who must be raised from the bottom of a well.” The image of the well is familiar throughout Gnostic traditions, from Mandaeism to Suhrawardi's “Tale of Exile” and the visionary writings of Najm Kobrâ. It prompts Mohammad Karîm-Khân to give a dramatic account of the ascent, from which I can retain only the conclusions here.

“We must reach the spiritual level at which the Friend, the Imam, becomes visible” (notice that the Imam, in Shiite language, is the very figure whom Sufism calls the mystical Beloved). “The Imam cannot come before we ourselves have arrived; we would not even see him. To acquire the capacity to see him is to rise higher, and to rise higher is to reach the place where the Imam becomes visible—the place the theosophers call Hûrqalyâ.”

The last things, then, and the Imam's return or parousia, are not an external event destined to erupt unexpectedly on some future day. They are a Presence progressively realized through acts that anticipate it. That is why the shaykh tells his reader: “You yourself, if you are capable of sensing it, will catch in the pages of this book, and in the words it contains, a fragrance carried from the flowers of the world of Hûrqalyâ.”

Shaykh Sarkâr Âghâ devoted an entire chapter of a substantial book to developing these pages. Where is Hûrqalyâ, this mundus imaginalis, this imaginal world? It is not quite the world of Plato's Ideas. It is the world of Image-Ideas, of the Forms and Figures of the sensible universe in a state of “subtle matter”—a world possessing extension, but made of pure light. It is reasonable to call it the “eighth clime,” beyond the “seven climes” that together comprise the earthly universe.

But we must not forget that it also lies within the unseen dimension of our own world: more precisely, within an invisible realm that becomes visible to inward sight once we understand how the eternal Forms belonging to the world of the Soul (Malakût) come into contact with the perishable materials of the sensible universe.

These Forms come into contact with the world in the same way that a human figure “enters” a mirror. The connection is incidental; there is nothing essential about the relationship. The mirror can break at any moment, and the connection can be severed.

In truth, the eternal Forms never “descend” from their own world, any more than a person actually “enters” a mirror, or the physical mass of the sun “descends” upon the Earth. What “comes into this world” from the eternal human soul is its outline, its image, its projected shadow. That image comes to the surface of the sensible mirror, and its appearance there is an act performed by the soul itself.

We have seen how five universes are layered within the scheme of worlds: the world of the Creative Imperative (the Lâhût, the fullness or pleroma of the Fourteen Immaculate Ones in their eternal substance); the world of the Intelligence; the world of Spirit (rûh), which forms an intermediate realm between the world of the Intelligence and the world of the Soul; the world of the Soul, which is the realm of the Forms of beings; and finally this visible, sensible world in which we now live, “the plane at which all the universes reach their final destination.

“The higher eternal Forms, those belonging to the world of the Soul, have reached this place. Here they have been hidden in the earthly dust of this world, although in another sense they have already departed from it. For this world is the tomb of the higher universes. All the beings inhabiting those other universes have been buried here, in this Earth.

“By the command of the Lord of the worlds, they must shake the dust from their heads and rise, delivered from their tomb. Each must find its own Dwelling again, must return home.” To leave the tomb is to leave behind all that decays and perishes, just as an image “leaves” a mirror when the mirror breaks.

We might note in passing that the oldest Ismaili Gnosis had already offered this inward meaning of the tomb. A saying attributed to the Prophet declares: “Between my tomb and the pulpit (minbar) from which I preach lies a garden among the gardens of paradise.”

A tenth-century Ismaili writer, Mohammad Sorkh of Nishapur, explains it as follows. This saying cannot be understood in its outward, literal sense. Ordinary people think only of a gravestone placed there: they look at it, pray before it, and call the place a “garden,” unaware that the saying can be understood only according to Gnostic truth, not its literal appearance.

The Prophet's pulpit represents precisely that literal appearance: the outward form of revealed religion, with its commands and doctrines. The tomb, meanwhile, represents philosophy. For in that tomb, the outward form of religion and its doctrines must undergo the decay and dissolution of death, just as a human material body decomposes in the grave. The garden of paradise between pulpit and tomb is the garden of Gnostic Truth: the field of resurrection from which the initiate's incorruptible Form arises.

Needless to say, this understanding is far removed from certain ideas about philosophy that prevailed in the medieval West, whether the Averroist doctrine of double truth or the theologians' conception of philosophy as ancilla theologiae, the handmaid of theology. Here philosophy marks a stage of initiation. It is indeed the “tomb” of theology, but only because the religion of spiritual wisdom (Dîn-e haqq) rises again from that in-between place—between dogma and tomb—where untransformed doctrinal belief must die and be transfigured. It is a new dawn, preceded by the night of death.

This corresponds exactly to the “being taken up into the heights” described by our Shaykhi authors. It does not mean, they tell us, abandoning this world, changing the present conditions of the physical body, flying off to some place in the sky, or having to undergo the exitus of physical death to escape this elemental earthly world, which our senses perceive.

Certainly, we must speak of a mystical death—the death evoked by so many traditions—which allows us to reach that other world even while we remain in this one. That is the whole point. We reach it when our eyes open to the other world and we are inwardly transformed into Hûrqalyâvis, people of Hûrqalyâ. Only then are we, in the true sense, companions of the Hidden Imam, equipped with the organs of perception belonging to the world beyond.

Shaykh Sarkâr Âghâ next asks us to grasp an image familiar both to the earliest Shiism and to Ismaili Gnosis: the appearance or parousia of the Resurrecting Imam as the day “when the Sun rises in the West.” We are told that this means the point and moment at which the present world completes its decline.
“We must never forget the true meaning,” the shaykh tells us, “which is the spiritual meaning.

“We must understand that our world has neither east nor west in itself, just as the sun has no rising or setting. What we call its revolution in its orbit is our own revolution, the revolution of human beings. Whenever we turn away from this world and advance spiritually toward the world beyond, the earthly world sinks toward its setting, while the light of the other world rises in the East.

“The east and west in question are east and west in their true sense: the spiritual East and West, independent of the compass points of sensible space—not the figurative east and west of our geography. A sun rising in the West therefore announces the hour of sunset, the final decline of this world. And that Light is the most sacred being of the Imam.”

These lines have far-reaching implications. Perhaps we are too ready to assume that a world arranged along a vertical axis, oriented toward a “celestial pole,” necessarily belongs to a geocentric picture of the universe, an imago mundi with the Earth at its center.

But we can observe what happens in a school such as Shaykhism when the heliocentric picture replaces the geocentric one. The Copernican revolution produces results rather different from those familiar to us. Understood in its spiritual meaning, heliocentrism now reveals what the true East is. The movement formerly understood in geocentric terms as the sun's revolution becomes the revolution of ourselves, the inhabitants of Earth.

Yet this is a revolution of our very being: as we advance toward our West, our decline and end, we move at the same time toward the East, the other world, our daybreak and our origin. Then it is the Earth that we see setting in the West: no longer the sunset, but the setting of the Earth. In a sense, this heliocentric revolution makes possible the ascent first projected and outlined within a geocentric vision.

We can go further. The insistence on spiritual meaning produces precisely the reversal of perspective described by Swedenborg when he relates the three meanings of divine Revelation to three universes: natural, spiritual, and celestial. What was above and at the origin—the celestial—had come to occupy the most deeply hidden center. What had thus been buried in the center now returns to its original place, in excelsis, on high.

Earthly time, the brief tomb in which the eternal Forms are confined, becomes their celestial space, through which they regain their origin. In this way there occurs a distinctive correspondence of forms—or better, a symmorphosis, a convergence into one form—between form in time and form in space. We first encountered a clue to this at the beginning of the present work, in the correspondence between perceiving forms in a mirror and a particular way of hearing the world musically. The same correspondence, in which time becomes space, was already suggested to us by Qâzî Sa'îd Qommî's commentary on the hadîth of the White Cloud.

This return from forms succeeding one another in time to forms that endure in space seems to be an essential movement of thought for anyone capable of “seeing things in Hûrqalyâ”: perceiving the dimensio mystica, the mystical dimension of beings and things, as already fully real. Such perception means grasping together what chronological time presents only in succession. The image of the “sun rising in the west,” whose significance for our Shaykhi authors we have just seen, is equally characteristic of Ismaili Gnosis, where it too is associated with the Imam's manifestation.
One further convergence between Shaykhi and Ismaili spiritual philosophy deserves mention.

However much the different branches of Shiism diverge in doctrine and position, they share a certain way of thinking. To speak of an eschatology already being fulfilled is to say, as we have seen, that every perception of the last things here and now is a perception of the dimensio mystica of beings and things: of a complete whole, even though that whole has not yet appeared within the successive order of chronological time.

To perceive its completeness already is, in one way or another, to perceive it no longer in time but in a space no longer ravaged by the endless coming and going of things. It is to perceive it in the space of Hûrqalyâ, and so to put an end to the conflict between time and space in which death triumphs.

The theme of the hexaemeron, the “six days of creation,” offers a striking example. Both Shaykhi and Ismaili thinkers discover a correspondence between temporal and spatial form. From another angle, this is an exercise of ta'wîl, spiritual interpretation, which here means “leading back” what is successive to what is simultaneous.

Once we have grasped the simultaneity to which the sequence of the “six days” can be returned, the “seventh day” in turn gives spatial form to the time of the Imam of the Resurrection (Qâ'im al-Qiyâmat). The “seventh day” ends the conflict between space and time. That is the aspect under which we must understand the relationship between eschatology and the correspondence of temporal and spatial forms—an aspect that, like many others in this book, I can do no more than briefly indicate.

Shaykh Ahmad Ahsâ'î, in his book of “Teachings” (Fawâ'id), whose first five chapters we examined earlier, offers a decisive interpretation of these “six days.” In two different ways he leads the temporal form of six successive days back to the spatial form of six universes existing simultaneously.

In broad outline, his first interpretation is this: the “six days” in which, according to Scripture, “God created the Heavens and the Earth” are the six worlds that make up the macrocosm. They are: (1) the world of the Intelligences; (2) the world of the Souls; (3) the world of Nature; (4) the world of the substances of the swirling cloud of atoms (al-habâ'), where each atom is the quantum of being invested in a particular existent—that is, the quantity of matter (maddâ) or light (nûr) which serves as the “father” of every being composed of matter and form; (5) the world of the Image (mithâl), the world of imaginal forms, which receive matter in its elemental state in this world and in its subtle state in the Malakût. These forms are the quiddities, the essential “whatnesses” or “mothers” of individual beings; and (6) the world of material bodies.

His second interpretation starts from the unchanging consistency of divine creation, which makes all these correspondences possible: “You will find no disharmony in the creation of the Merciful” (Qur'an 67:3). The shaykh understands the “six days” as belonging to the “second creation” (a technical expression we explained earlier). They are the constitutive elements present in every being. None of these “days,” therefore, can appear before the others.

All are given together, along with the matter that provides a being's quantum of existence (light, its “father”) and the form that provides its quantum of quiddity (Mercy, its “mother”). The shaykh names them using the same terms that logic applies to the predicaments or categories. He expressly insists, however, that he means something quite different by those terms: in the ordinary list of logical categories, they refer only to accidents added to a substance. To keep the terminology precise, I shall use the traditional Latin names here.

We therefore have another series of six—a group of six which, in certain respects, corresponds to the first. The shaykh bases this interpretation on hadîth from the Sixth and Eighth Imams. The six “days” that constitute the structure of every being are as follows:
The first day is the quantum (kamm, quantity): the particular measure of being or substance (qadar jawharî) allotted to each being.
The second day is the quale (kayf): quality or mode, with its various specifications.

The third day is the quando (waqt), or when. Here the shaykh distinguishes three categories. They are founded on a distinction we already encountered in Qâzî Sa'îd Qommî, who differentiates opaque time, subtle time, and absolutely subtle time. But Shaykh Ahmad develops this distinction in a remarkable way. He places those three degrees within each of the three orders of duration: chronological time, sempiternity, and eternity.

a) First comes chronological time (zamân), which has three degrees: subtle, intermediate, and dense. These correspond to different states of the body, from subtle bodies to material bodies—for example, the Sphere of Spheres, the other celestial Spheres, and the body of the sublunary world.

b) Next comes dahr (aevum, aiôn), sempiternity, which likewise has three states: subtle, the time of the Jabarût or world of the Intelligences; intermediate, the time of the Malakût or world of the Souls; and opaque or dense, the time of the “substances of the swirling cloud of atoms.”

c) Lastly comes sarmad, eternity. It too has three degrees, corresponding to the moments of the fourfold Creative Act discussed earlier (p. 269): subtle, the time of mashî'at, the primordial Will; intermediate, the time of the prestructuring of beings (taqdîr, handasa wojûdîya); and dense or opaque, corresponding to the “decree” (qazâ) and the “signature” (imzâ).

The fourth day is the ubi (makân), or where: place, the “vessel containing whatever flows into it.” Its modes correspond in structure to those of the quando. There is an eternal place (sarmadî) for eternal realities (sarmadîyât), a sempiternal place (dahrî) for sempiternal realities (dahrîyât), and a temporal place (zamânî) for temporal realities (zamânîyât).

The fifth day is situs, or jihat: the orientation (tawajjoh) of a being toward its principle, and of that principle toward the being. It is also the sense or direction in which the being extends outward from its origin.
The sixth day is rank (roiba): the position, nearer to or farther from its source, of the influence received by a being.

It is easy to see that the third and fourth “days,” as Shaykh Ahmad analyzes them, already give thought everything it needs to establish the correspondence between forms in time and forms in space. They thus make it possible to transform time into space—or, in eschatological terms, to pass from the time of this world into the time of another world that brings the first to an end. Unfortunately we cannot pursue the matter here.

We must be content to set out the striking convergence, the shared movement of thought, between Shaykhi and Ismaili spiritual philosophy, particularly as we find it in the great Iranian Ismaili thinker Nâsir-e Khosraw.

Naturally, a thinker such as Nâsir-e Khosraw makes no secret of his impatience with the pious chatter of literalists. Those who practice spiritual interpretation (ahl-e ta'wîl) hold that God's Book is a guide to the spiritual life. And it is hard to see what spiritual benefit anyone could gain from learning merely that the physical heavens and earth did not once exist, that the Creator then needed no fewer than six days to produce them, and that afterward he took his seat on a throne.

Ismaili thinkers—above all Abû Ya'qûb Sejestânî in the tenth century and Nâsir-e Khosraw in the eleventh—therefore apply an interpretation operating at two higher levels of meaning: the esoteric and the esoteric within the esoteric. At each level “time becomes space,” and what succeeds one thing after another is understood as existing simultaneously.

In its outward sense, a “day” is the time the sun takes to travel from the eastern horizon to the western horizon. That measure of time corresponds to the extent of the Earth's surface covered by its light.

But this relationship merely measures how Nature (tabî'at, physis) works in the world through its powers. These powers are six in number: movement and rest, matter and form, time and place. Our Ismaili authors therefore make the following distinction. Outwardly, “day” means the sun's illumination of the world as it moves from east to west. Inwardly, the first day is Nature's illumination of the world through movement; the second, through rest; the third, through Matter; the fourth, through Form; the fifth, through time; and the sixth, through space.
The effects and traces of these six “days-as-powers” remain permanently impressed upon every being and every thing in the material world. Each expresses them according to its own inward law.
